title: The Old Stone Bridge
summary: A crumbling single-span bridge over a narrow river gorge. Locals swear they hear footsteps crossing at night, but the bridge is always empty when they look.
body: A crumbling single-span bridge arches over a narrow river gorge. The stone is slick with moss and the parapet is chipped where carts have scraped it for generations.

After sundown, locals claim they hear footsteps and the creak of unseen weight crossing from bank to bank. Lantern light shows nothing, and any attempt to wait on the bridge feels like being watched from below.
Use this as a travel encounter that can turn into combat, negotiation, or a social mystery depending on what is haunting the bridge.
hooks: Travelers vanish when crossing after sundown.
A rival party swears they were pushed by an invisible hand mid-crossing.
A local begs the party to retrieve a charm tossed into the river years ago.
complications: The bridge shudders and cracks if angered or disrespected.
The river below carries bones and broken gear from past incidents.
The haunting is a misdirect for something living under the water.
rewards: A hidden cache wedged under a loose stone.
A blessing for safe crossing in this region.
A clue pointing to a larger threat upstream.

title: Emberglass Cavern
special_element: **The cavern runs hotter with depth, and the heat is stored, not made.** No fire burns down there, no mineral vein explains it. The glass holds warmth the way a hearth does after the flame has gone out — and the deeper you go, the older and stronger that borrowed warmth gets. Whatever banked it did so a very long time ago, and it has not cooled.
summary: Category: Location · Tier: 2 · Difficulty: hard · Biome: cavern · Mood: wondrous
body: Category: Location · Tier: 2 · Difficulty: hard · Biome: cavern · Mood: wondrous

The tunnel narrows, then opens into a cave built of black glass. Every wall is soot-dark crystal, faceted like a thousand mirrors turned away from the light, and the air is warm — not damp cave-warm, but *hearth*-warm, the way a room feels after the fire's been going all afternoon. Torchlight comes back off the facets gold instead of white.
Walk deeper and the warmth climbs. A cave should get colder the further you go from the sky. This one doesn't.

Emberglass Cavern is a vein of glassy black stone that formed, by all evidence, around something that burned for a very long time. Prospectors who mapped the outer chambers found the crystal cool to the touch at the mouth and close to skin-scalding two hundred feet in — a gradient that runs backwards from every cave anyone has surveyed.

The glass fractures into curved, obsidian-sharp shards. Miners working the outer seams describe a low, resiny warmth coming off a freshly-broken face, like standing too close to banked coals. Nobody has mapped the deep chambers and come back with a full account of what is down there.

Decide before play what banked the heat at the bottom of the gradient — a dormant elemental, a buried forge from an age nobody remembers, or nothing at all, just glass that remembers fire the way old wood remembers the axe. None of it needs revealing on this visit. The gradient is the hook; the answer is the second visit.

Push the heat as a real cost past two hundred feet: exhaustion, water skins gone hot and foul, glass too hot to grip bare-handed. Rule the deep chambers as difficult terrain for anyone in metal armour. This is a hard site because the environment is the antagonist — there is no monster waiting in the dark unless you put one there.

Special element: **The cavern runs hotter with depth, and the heat is stored, not made.** No fire burns down there, no mineral vein explains it. The glass holds warmth the way a hearth does after the flame has gone out — and the deeper you go, the older and stronger that borrowed warmth gets. Whatever banked it did so a very long time ago, and it has not cooled.
complications: Hooks: a mining concern wants a survey team to find how deep the warm seam runs; a scholar insists the reversed gradient breaks a law of nature and wants first-hand notes; the prospector who went furthest in came back and will not say what the heat sounded like.
Complications: shards fracture underfoot and open thin cuts that cauterise as they open; the thickened air slows any spell needing a clear breath; torches sweat and gutter near the hottest walls.
Rewards: raw emberglass sells well to jewellers and alchemists for its colour; a fist-sized shard cut from the deep chambers stays warm in the hand for days.

title: Tideworn Chapel
special_element: The chapel rebuilds its interior — altar, icon, offerings, and the blank face of the statue — to answer whatever the person walking through the door most needs, and it has never once guessed wrong. Nobody has worked out how it knows.
summary: Category: Location · Tier: 1 · Biome: coast · Difficulty: easy · Mood: wondrous
body: Category: Location · Tier: 1 · Biome: coast · Difficulty: easy · Mood: wondrous

A small stone chapel sits above the tideline, its driftwood pews bleached grey, salt crusting every sill. Inside, you can hear the sea — a slow wash and pull, in and out — though the water is fifty feet below and the door has been shut all winter. The air smells of wax and brine. Over the altar stands a carved figure whose face was never finished: smooth stone where the features should be.
Fishing families up and down the coast use the chapel, and none of them agree on which god it belongs to. Ask three worshippers and you get three answers, each delivered with total confidence.
They are not lying. No one enters the chapel the same way twice. Between visits the building keeps its walls, its pews, and the sound of the sea — everything else moves.

A sailor finds carved fish heaped for a sea-mother. A widow finds a shrine hung with mourning cloth cut for her exact loss. A child looking for courage finds a painted knight above the altar. No one has ever caught it changing. The door opens and it is already different.
The chapel is not the Red Stag Trail. The Trail moves you toward the thing you want and charges you for the walk; the chapel gives nothing, takes nothing, and only says the thing out loud.

Decide before play what the chapel shows each visiting character, and why — it must reflect something true about them, not a random image. The chapel grants insight, never mechanical benefit; resist turning it into a vending machine for buffs and answers. The pressure here is social, not tactical: the cost of entering is that your party sees what you needed. Variant: if you want the place hungrier, let the statue's face finish itself a little more with every visitor it reads correctly.

Special element: The chapel rebuilds its interior — altar, icon, offerings, and the blank face of the statue — to answer whatever the person walking through the door most needs, and it has never once guessed wrong. Nobody has worked out how it knows.
complications: Hooks: a grieving villager insists the party visit "their" chapel and see what it shows them; a scholar pays good coin to anyone who can catch the interior changing.
Complications: two characters enter together and each sees a different room; argue about it in front of the statue and the doors seal until the arguing stops.

Rewards: the room a character walks into names a truth they had never said aloud — and it names it in front of whoever came in with them. The party leaves knowing something about each other they were not told: a rumour, a place, or a piece of a companion's past.

title: Red Stag Trail
special_element: The trail leads each walker, separately, toward the thing they most want — and it splits the party without any of them noticing. Five people set off shoulder to shoulder, certain they never lost sight of each other, and arrive at five different places hours apart. Only afterward, comparing the walk, does anyone realise they were never on the same path at all.
summary: Category: Location · Tier: 2 · Biome: forest · Difficulty: medium · Mood: mysterious
body: Category: Location · Tier: 2 · Biome: forest · Difficulty: medium · Mood: mysterious

The trail is barely a trail — a deer-track of packed leaf-mould, silent underfoot, smelling of wet bark and something sweeter beneath it, like fruit left too long in the sun. Sunlight comes down in coin-sized patches. And somewhere behind you, without anyone ever deciding to stop talking, your companions have gone quiet.

The Red Stag Trail runs through a stretch of ancient forest that no two maps agree on. Locals know not to walk it alone, and know better than to walk it in a hurry. It is not lost — it simply does not go where you think it goes.

Travellers describe walking single file for an afternoon and arriving somewhere none of them meant to. A hunter chasing a stag comes out at the edge of a lake he swears was never in this wood. A merchant taking a shortcut to market steps out an hour later at his own front door.
Nothing on the trail attacks. Whatever tends it wants people walking, not running.

Decide before play what each PC's "want" resolves to — keep it small and personal (a person, a place, an answer), not campaign-ending. Use the split to peel one PC away for a private scene, or to quietly reunite the party if their wants align. Never announce the split; let the players find it when someone says "wait — when did we get here?" Variant: run the trail as a single shared path that leads only to the party's loudest want, if you'd rather not break the group up.

Special element: The trail leads each walker, separately, toward the thing they most want — and it splits the party without any of them noticing. Five people set off shoulder to shoulder, certain they never lost sight of each other, and arrive at five different places hours apart. Only afterward, comparing the walk, does anyone realise they were never on the same path at all.
complications: Hooks: a search party insists their missing hunter "just walked into the trees and never came out the other side"; a merchant caravan hires an escort through the wood and doesn't know to warn anyone.
Complications: a PC's own want pulls them off course mid-scene, with no moment where the group actually separated; whatever the party is chasing may have left the same way.
Rewards: a walker who reaches what they wanted sometimes finds it waiting, faintly changed — a lost person, a lost coin, a lost certainty — and the wood asks nothing for it. Yet.

title: Library of Salt
special_element: Every shape in the salt drifts was once a person who read too long. The library preserves its readers the way it preserves its pages — slowly, from the fingertips inward — and every hour spent absorbed in a text is an hour spent becoming one more curve in the floor. There is no ritual and no curse to break. It is simply patient, and it is still hungry.
summary: Category: Location · Tier: 3 · Difficulty: hard · Biome: ruins · Mood: melancholy
body: Category: Location · Tier: 3 · Difficulty: hard · Biome: ruins · Mood: melancholy

Salt has swallowed the Library of Salt. The shelves are sagging white ridges now, crusted thick as bone, sloping down into drifts that reach the knee. The air tastes of brine before it tastes of anything else — dry, mineral, catching at the back of the throat with every breath. The drifts underfoot do not shift like sand. They hold their shape: a curve here like a bent shoulder, a hollow there like a cupped hand, pressed into the salt and never disturbed. No wind moves through the broken roof, and yet, somewhere below the floor, the salt sighs.

Before the collapse this was a great reading hall — vaulted stone, shelving from floor to ceiling, a place scholars travelled seasons to reach. What toppled it wasn't fire or war. The salt came from within, seeping up through the floor stones over decades: first a fine crust on the lowest shelves, then drifts that buried whole aisles. Most of the books are gone, dissolved or entombed. What's left are salt-white pages, brittle as old bone, scattered loose across the ridgelines.

The hall is treacherous. Ceiling sections groan and shed dust at a raised voice, and a drift-bank can slump and swallow a careless step. Torch flame leans and gutters in the salt-damp air for no reason the DM needs to explain.

Anyone who stays and reads — really reads, page after page, hour after hour — starts to notice their own knuckles drying, their voice roughening like a throat full of dust. The library does not want visitors. It wants readers who don't leave.

Decide before play how long a character can read before the salt starts taking them — a clean, visible countdown (one mark per hour of in-fiction reading) works better than a hidden save. Let the players watch a companion's hand pale and stiffen well before it matters mechanically; the horror is in seeing it happen, not in the moment it's confirmed. This is the site the *Salt That Was Words* and the *Salt-Sheet Riddle* were dug out of, not a retelling of either: the lore is where the salt came from, the riddle is one page read closely, and this place is what the reading costs by the hour. Run it cold — neither is required at the table.

Special element: Every shape in the salt drifts was once a person who read too long. The library preserves its readers the way it preserves its pages — slowly, from the fingertips inward — and every hour spent absorbed in a text is an hour spent becoming one more curve in the floor. There is no ritual and no curse to break. It is simply patient, and it is still hungry.
complications: Hooks: a scholar's family hires the party to retrieve someone who went in three weeks ago and never came out · a fragment of salt-page turns up in a market stall, still faintly legible.
Complications: a character becomes absorbed in a text and loses track of time — track it openly, in hours, not narrative beats · the ceiling sheds a section if anyone shouts or fights inside.

Rewards: intact salt-pages hold genuinely lost knowledge, worth real coin to the right buyer · one drift, excavated carefully, yields a reader's untouched satchel — their tools, their notes, their name.

title: Hollow Ward Post
special_element: Travellers who spend the night hear the bell ring once before dawn: a single clear toll from above the empty lintel. The warning is always true. Whatever danger the road holds that day — a predator on the trail, a washed-out ford, a patrol with wrong intentions — the bell rings first. Nobody who passes through asks about it twice.
summary: Category: Location · Region: state1 · Difficulty: easy · Mood: unsettling
body: Category: Location · Region: state1 · Difficulty: easy · Mood: unsettling

A squat stone post where the frontier road narrows — walls the colour of old ash, a rusted iron bracket above the lintel where a bell once hung. Inside, woodsmoke and sage still hang in the air, and the kettle on its hook holds water warm to the touch. The hearth holds only cold grey ash. There is no other door.

The waypost was built to log traveller traffic on the frontier road, and it did, for a generation. The Frontier Watch was disbanded — nobody out here agrees on exactly when — and the post was quietly abandoned. Travellers still use it as a shelter, and whatever they find inside, they leave as they found it. Out here that habit has a name: *the customs of the road.*
A duty ledger hangs on a peg by the door. The last signed entry is dated three weeks ago, and the page is not quite full.
The iron bracket above the lintel held the alarm bell. It was taken down before the post closed — lost, repurposed, nobody agrees. The bracket has been empty for years.

Decide before play whether the bell rings that night. If it does, have something true waiting on the road — bad weather, a predator, an ambush. The bell is never a bluff: honour it every time, and the players learn to trust it. That trust is the hook.

The kettle and the bell are separate beats. Run *The Kettle's Still Warm* first if you want the post unsettling from the moment they arrive; let the bell come later, in the dark, after they have stopped wondering who made the fire.

Do not explain the bell unless the players pursue it hard. A partial answer — *"the old watch-captain who last rang it is buried on the ridge somewhere, they say"* — gives them something to hold without closing the question.

Special element: Travellers who spend the night hear the bell ring once before dawn: a single clear toll from above the empty lintel. The warning is always true. Whatever danger the road holds that day — a predator on the trail, a washed-out ford, a patrol with wrong intentions — the bell rings first. Nobody who passes through asks about it twice.
complications: **Hooks:** The ledger's last entry carries a name the party recognises. · The kettle is warm with no fire to explain it (→ *The Kettle's Still Warm*). · A bedroll on the bunk has been slept in since the last rain.

**Complications:** The bell rings mid-afternoon, not before dawn — something on the road ahead is not following the old rules. · A rider pulls in hard and fast, wanting walls between themselves and the road, not yet willing to say what is behind them.

**Rewards:** The ledger holds route notes going back years — terrain, flood dates, patrol schedules, warnings left by travellers who knew the road. · A sealed tin box under the bunk, addressed *DELIVER IF FOUND* to a name in a town two days east.
